steps.name: Quiz: Secure Sharing

answers.text: Password managers provide encrypted sharing with audit trails, and credentials are never exposed in plain text to the channel
answers.explanation: Password managers encrypt credentials end-to-end, limit access to specific recipients, maintain audit logs of who accessed what, and ensure sensitive data never appears in searchable chat history.

answers.text: Password managers are faster to use than typing credentials in a chat
answers.explanation: Speed is not the primary benefit. The key advantage is security - encrypted sharing, access controls, and audit trails that prevent unauthorized exposure.

answers.text: Collaboration channels automatically delete messages after 24 hours, but password managers keep them forever
answers.explanation: Most collaboration channels retain messages indefinitely, which is actually part of the problem. Password managers are better because they provide controlled, encrypted access rather than broadcasting credentials.

answers.text: Password managers only work on company devices, so the credentials can't be accessed from personal devices
answers.explanation: Password managers can be accessed from various devices. Their security comes from encryption, access controls, and audit trails - not device restrictions.

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Collaboration tools like WorkStream, Slack, and Teams are essential for teamwork - but they are not designed for sharing sensitive information. Channels can have hidden audiences that you may not be aware of. Share credentials securely:
  • Never post credentials, API keys, or secrets in channels - use a password manager's secure sharing feature instead
  • Direct colleagues to the vault - when someone asks for credentials in a channel, point them to the password manager
  • Use the right tool - credentials belong in a password vault, not in chat messages
Maintain channel hygiene:
  • Audit integrations regularly - remove webhooks, bots, and apps that are no longer needed
  • Review memberships quarterly - remove former contractors, departed team members, and external guests whose projects have ended
  • Use the principle of least privilege - only add members and integrations that are actively needed for current work
If credentials are exposed:
  • Rotate immediately - change the compromised credentials without delay, because rotation is the only step that actually revokes the attacker's access
  • Report to IT Security - report before you clean up, so the team can see the message, the channel and the audience for themselves; even if no breach has occurred yet, reporting enables proactive monitoring
  • Remove the message last - clear the sensitive content from the channel once IT Security has what it needs, and remember deletion does not remove it from compliance exports or anyone's screenshots

steps.name: Understanding Steganography

highlighterTexts: Steganography is the practice of hiding data within other data. In cybersecurity, attackers conceal malicious code inside ordinary-looking files like images.
Unlike encryption (which makes data unreadable), steganography makes the hidden data completely invisible. The carrier file appears perfectly normal.
Stegosploit hides malicious JavaScript in image pixel color values. The image appears normal but contains executable code.
When the image loads, a script uses the HTML5 Canvas API to read the hidden payload back out of the pixels, then runs it.

Attackers deliver these attacks through links in emails and messages to pages they control, and through compromised websites (banner ads, thumbnails). The page supplies the script; the image supplies the hidden code.
Any image you encounter online could potentially contain hidden code - this is why security tools that scan image content are essential.

steps.name: Protection Strategies

highlighterTexts: Technical defenses: keep browsers updated, use endpoint protection that scans for steganographic content, and disable automatic image loading in email.

steps.description:
The training outlines essential protection strategies against image-based attacks: 1. Technical Defenses
  • Keep browsers and applications updated (patches close the browser flaws these payloads exploit)
  • Use endpoint protection that scans for steganographic content
  • Enable browser security features and content security policies
  • Disable automatic image loading in email clients when possible
2. Safe Handling Practices
  • Be cautious with links from unknown senders, especially to their own sites
  • Verify sender identity through separate channels before opening their links
  • Use official portfolio platforms (Behance, Dribbble) rather than the sender's own site
  • When in doubt, ask IT to check the link first
3. Organizational Controls
  • Email gateways that analyze image content for suspicious patterns
  • Sandboxing that opens attachments in isolated environments
  • Regular security awareness training for employees handling visual content

Alice has completed the Image-Based Attacks & Steganography training. The key lessons from this experience are clear:

  • Steganography hides code in pixels - The image looks normal but contains malicious payloads
  • Browser features can be misused - A script can use the Canvas API to read hidden code out of pixels
  • A block is not an all-clear - The alert proved an attack; closing it without reporting let the part that got through do its damage
  • The email was the lure, the page was the attack - Email clients do not run scripts; the danger was the link
  • Verify before clicking - Use official platforms and verify unknown senders
  • Minutes matter - The 45-minute delay between closing the alert and reporting gave the attacker time to access client files
steps.instructions: Click Next to proceed to the quiz.

description: Steganography hides code inside an image without visibly changing it, and the attack needs a web page to run. Learn the warning signs of an unsolicited link to a sender's own site, why a security alert that says blocked must still be reported, and what to do if a suspicious image has been opened.

name: Insider Threat (Accidental)

quiz.text: What is the most common cause of accidental insider threat incidents?

answers.text: Malicious employees stealing data
Human error such as misdirected emails, wrong attachments, or misconfigured permissions
Hackers breaking through firewalls
Software bugs that expose data automatically

quiz.text: Alice sent confidential salary data to an external client by mistake. Which action by Alice was the MOST important factor in preventing a full data breach?

answers.text: The DLP system flagged the email
Alice reported the incident immediately, giving the security team time to contain it
The client happened to not open the attachment
The file was password-protected

quiz.text: Which of the following are effective practices for preventing accidental data exposure? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Verify the recipient, attachment, and content before clicking Send
Enable a send delay in your email settings
Keep sensitive files in a separate, clearly labeled folder
Rely entirely on the DLP system to catch mistakes
Avoid sending emails before your first cup of coffee

answers.text: Public
Internal

Wait a few days to see if anyone notices

steps.description: It's Monday morning and your calendar is packed. You have a compensation review meeting with HR on Wednesday, and a client proposal that was due last Friday. Your inbox is overflowing and you're already behind.
steps.instructions: Click Next to continue.

Attached is the Q3 compensation review spreadsheet for the Analytics department. This file contains salary figures, bonus allocations, and performance ratings for all 47 team members.

Please review it before Wednesday's meeting. As a reminder, this data is classified as Restricted under our data handling policy and should not be shared outside HR and approved managers.

Thanks,
Priya Sharma
HR Business Partner
email.subject: CONFIDENTIAL: Q3 Compensation Review Data

steps.description: An email arrives from Priya Sharma in Human Resources with the Q3 compensation data Alice needs for Wednesday's meeting.
steps.instructions: Read the email from HR.

steps.name: The Waiting Client
steps.note: When sensitive files and routine work share the same inbox, the risk of a mix-up increases dramatically. This is why data classification and careful file handling matter.

highlighterTexts: This email contains restricted compensation data for 47 employees. Handle it with care.

steps.description: Alice notices the confidential warning in the HR email. She saves the spreadsheet to her downloads for the Wednesday meeting.
steps.instructions: Read the email and download the attachment.

steps.name: The Rushed Reply

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Just following up on the Q3 analytics proposal. Our leadership team meets tomorrow afternoon to finalize vendor selections, so I'd need the proposal and supporting data by end of day today if possible.

I know you mentioned it was nearly ready last week. Could you send it over when you get a chance?

Thanks,
James Porter
Director of Operations, Pinnacle Corp
email.subject: Re: Q3 Analytics Proposal - Following Up

highlighterTexts: James needs the proposal by end of day today for tomorrow's vendor decision. A deadline like this is exactly when people rush the reply.
He asks for the proposal and its supporting data, nothing else. Whatever you attach should be exactly that file.

variables.name: replyMessage
variables.correctValue: Hi James, apologies for the delay! Here's the spreadsheet with the Q3 data. Let me know if you need anything else before tomorrow's meeting.

steps.description: Another message arrives - James Porter at Pinnacle Corp needs the project proposal by end of day. Under pressure, Alice rushes to reply. Both files are in her downloads - the confidential HR spreadsheet and the client proposal. In her rush, she grabs the wrong one.
steps.instructions: Read the client email, then reply and attach the requested file.

steps.name: DLP Alert

email.message:
Data Loss Prevention Alert

An outgoing email from your account has been flagged for containing sensitive data.

Sender: alice@brightpathanalytics.com
Recipient: james.porter@pinnaclecorp.com (EXTERNAL)
Subject: Re: Q3 Analytics Proposal - Following Up
Attachment: Q3_Compensation_Review_CONFIDENTIAL.xlsx

Classification Match: RESTRICTED - Employee Compensation Data
Policy Violated: DLP-Policy-003: Restricted data must not be sent to external recipients
Status: Email delivered - not blocked

Action Required: This email was delivered before the DLP scan completed. You must report this incident immediately through the Security Portal.

Do NOT attempt to handle this independently. Contact the Security Operations team.
email.subject: ALERT: Sensitive Data Detected in Outgoing Email

highlighterTexts: The DLP system detected restricted employee compensation data in an outgoing email to an external recipient. The email was already delivered before it could be blocked.
Alice must report this incident immediately through the Security Portal, not try to handle it alone.

steps.description:
Minutes later, an automated alert appears in Alice's inbox. The company's Data Loss Prevention system has flagged her outgoing email.

Alice's stomach drops. She just sent the entire Analytics department's salary data - names, compensation figures, bonus amounts, and performance ratings for 47 colleagues - to an external client.

This isn't a phishing attack. There's no malicious actor. Alice made a simple, human mistake under time pressure. But the consequences are just as real as any cyberattack.

Most insider incidents come from careless mistakes, not malice: misdirected emails, misconfigured permissions, lost devices.
steps.instructions: Read the alert from the DLP system.

steps.name: The Realization

answers.text: Try to recall the email using the email system's recall feature
answers.explanation: Email recall is unreliable, especially for external recipients. The email has already been delivered. The priority is to report the incident so the security team can begin containment - including contacting the recipient directly.

answers.text: Report the incident immediately through the security portal
answers.explanation: Immediate reporting gives the security team the best chance to contain the exposure. They can contact the recipient, assess regulatory obligations, and begin the response process. Speed is critical - every minute counts.

answers.text: Email the client asking them to delete the file and not open it
answers.explanation: While the client should eventually be contacted, doing it yourself without coordinating with the security team can create legal complications. The security team has protocols for handling external data exposure - let them manage the communication.

answers.text: Wait until tomorrow to see if the client notices the wrong attachment
answers.explanation: Waiting is the worst option. Every hour of delay increases the risk of the data being opened, forwarded, or saved. Regulatory frameworks like GDPR require prompt notification. Delayed reporting can turn a containable incident into a full-blown breach.

data.question: Alice just realized she sent confidential salary data to an external client. What should she do FIRST?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Reporting the Incident
steps.description: Alice knows she needs to act fast. She opens the Security Portal to file a report.
steps.instructions: Log in to the Security Portal.

steps.name: Filing the Incident Report
steps.note: When reporting a data incident, focus on facts: what data, who received it, when it happened, and how. Don't minimize or speculate - accurate reporting helps the security team respond effectively.

variables.correctValue:

steps.name: Security Operations Response

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Thank you for reporting this immediately. Your quick action gave us the best possible window to respond. Here's what we've done so far:
  • Recipient contacted: Our legal team reached out to James Porter at Pinnacle Corp. He confirmed the attachment was not opened and has permanently deleted the email under a signed acknowledgment.
  • DLP hold: We've placed a temporary hold on outgoing emails from your account containing Restricted-classified attachments until additional safeguards are in place.
  • Regulatory assessment: Because the data was confirmed deleted before being accessed, this qualifies as a contained incident rather than a reportable breach. No regulatory notification is required.
Please review the full incident analysis at security.brightpathanalytics.com/incident-review. There are also some prevention tools we'd like you to enable.

This could have been much worse. Your immediate report made all the difference.

Nathan Cole
Security Operations Center
email.subject: Re: Incident INC-2024-0847 - Misdirected Email Update

highlighterTexts: Reporting at once gave the team its best window: the recipient confirmed the file was never opened and deleted it under a signed acknowledgment.
A temporary hold now stops Restricted attachments leaving Alice's account until more safeguards are in place.
Because the data was deleted before anyone accessed it, this counts as a contained incident, not a reportable breach.

steps.description: An hour later, Alice receives an email from the Security Operations team with an update on the incident.
steps.instructions: Read the response from the Security team.

steps.name: Incident Review
steps.description: Alice opens the incident review dashboard to understand the full scope of what happened and what could have gone wrong.
steps.instructions: Click the incident review link in the email, look the page over, then click Next.

steps.name: Understanding the Exposure

highlighterTexts: What was exposed: Full names, job titles, base salaries, bonus amounts and performance ratings for 47 employees.
Under most privacy regulations, employee compensation data counts as personally identifiable information (PII).
If this had not been contained: mandatory breach notification to all 47 affected employees, and possible regulatory fines under data protection laws.
On top of that: lost employee trust, possible legal action and reputational damage with the external client.
Root cause: The wrong file was attached because the salary data and the proposal sat in the same downloads folder with similar recent timestamps.
No pre-send check was done, and the DLP system detected the violation but could not block it before delivery.

steps.description:
The incident review page shows exactly what data was exposed and what the consequences could have been if the recipient had opened the file.

Understanding data classification is the first step to preventing accidental exposure. Every file Alice handles should be treated according to its classification level.
steps.instructions: Review the highlighted sections of the incident analysis.

steps.name: Data Classification Check

answers.text: Public - approved for external sharing
answers.explanation: Public data includes marketing materials, press releases, and published reports. Salary data is never public - sharing it externally is exactly what caused this incident.

answers.text: Internal - for employees only
answers.explanation: Internal data includes general business information like org charts and policies. Salary data is more sensitive - it contains personal financial information that could cause harm if exposed.

answers.text: Confidential - sensitive business data
answers.explanation: Confidential includes client contracts and strategic plans. Salary data goes one step further because it contains personal financial information tied to specific individuals.

answers.text: Restricted - highest sensitivity, strict controls required
answers.explanation: Employee compensation data is classified as Restricted because it contains personally identifiable financial information. Restricted data requires encryption, access controls, and must never be sent to external recipients without explicit authorization.

data.question: Which data classification level applies to employee salary and performance data?

steps.instructions: Answer the question.

steps.name: Prevention Tools

highlighterTexts: Verify before you send. Before clicking Send on any email with attachments, check three things: (1) Is the recipient correct? (2) Is it the right file? (3) Does it contain anything the recipient should not see?
This 10-second check prevents the most common accidental data exposure.

Enable send delay. Most email clients offer a 1-2 minute delay before sending. This gives you a window to catch mistakes. Brightpath's email system supports a configurable delay under Settings > Mail > Undo Send.

Separate sensitive and routine files. Keep restricted files in a dedicated, clearly labeled folder - not in your general downloads. When sensitive data lives next to everyday files, mix-ups are inevitable.

steps.description: The incident review includes prevention recommendations that Alice should adopt. These are practical habits and tools that reduce the risk of accidental data exposure.
steps.instructions: Open the prevention tools, look them over, then click Next and review the highlighted recommendations.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description: Congratulations on completing the Accidental Insider Threat training. Before you send: Always verify three things before clicking Send on emails with attachments - the recipient, the attachment, and the content. This 10-second habit prevents the most common accidental data exposure. Enable send delay in your email settings for an extra safety net. If it happens: Report immediately. Do not try to fix it yourself, recall the email, or wait to see what happens. Alice's immediate report gave the security team enough time to contain the exposure before the file was opened. Every minute of delay increases the risk. Know your data: Understand what classification level applies to the files you handle. Restricted data (salary, PII, financial records) requires extra care - dedicated folders, encryption, and strict access controls. Treat every file according to its sensitivity. Organize your workspace: Keep sensitive files separated from routine work. A dedicated "Restricted" folder with clear naming prevents the kind of mix-up that caused this incident. If sensitive data lives next to everyday files, accidents are just a matter of time. DLP is a safety net, not a solution: Data Loss Prevention systems catch many mistakes, but they can't block every email before delivery. Your own habits are the first and most reliable line of defense.

description: Many data exposures are accidental: a wrong attachment or a rushed reply sends confidential data outside the company. Learn the habits that cause them, the safeguards that prevent them such as checking attachments and a send delay, and why an accidental exposure must still be reported immediately.

Backup IT infrastructure for emergencies
IT security monitoring tools

answers.text: Use it right away to meet the deadline
Check if IT has an approved alternative or submit a software request
Ask other colleagues if they are using it
Use it only for non-sensitive data

Client contracts requiring specific data handling may be violated

IT deleted them remotely
The client rejected them due to format issues

steps.name: A Tight Deadline

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Just checking in on the design deliverables. Our review board meets Friday, so we'll need the final files by end of day Thursday at the latest.

Can you send them over as soon as they're ready? Just share a download link and I'll grab them.

Thanks,
Sarah
email.subject: RE: Project Deliverables - Ready for Review?

highlighterTexts: The client needs the files by Thursday end of day for a Friday review board, so there is time pressure from the start.
She asks for a download link, and the team's usual platform cannot take files this size. That gap is where unapproved tools tend to show up.

steps.description: Your team has finalized the design files for the Hawthorne project, but there's a problem - the files total 127MB, and the file-sharing platform your team normally uses only handles up to 50MB. The client is already asking for the files.
steps.instructions: Read the email from the client.

steps.name: A Message from Marcus

telegramMessage.text: Hey Alice! Heard you're stuck on the file size thing with Hawthorne. I've been using this free tool called CloudDrop for months - handles files up to 5GB, no IT ticket needed. Want me to send you the link?

steps.description: Alice's phone buzzes with a Telegram notification from her colleague Marcus Chen.

steps.name: Getting the Link
steps.note: Shadow IT refers to any technology used within an organization without explicit IT approval. It includes cloud services, apps, browser extensions, and software that employees adopt on their own.

telegramMessage.text: Here you go: clouddrop.io - Just drag and drop your files. No account needed, works up to 5GB. Half our team uses it for client stuff!

variables.name: reply

steps.name: Opening CloudDrop
steps.note: Free file-sharing services often have minimal security controls, unclear data residency policies, and no enterprise compliance certifications.
steps.description: Alice opens CloudDrop on her desktop browser. The site looks professional and straightforward - a clean interface promising fast, free file sharing.
steps.instructions: Navigate to CloudDrop in your browser.

steps.name: A Disturbing Email

email.message:
Dear CloudDrop User,

We are writing to inform you that CloudDrop experienced a security incident. An unauthorized party gained access to our file storage infrastructure.

What happened: A vulnerability in our storage system allowed unauthorized access to user files.

What was affected: Files uploaded during this period may have been accessed or downloaded by the unauthorized party.

What we are doing: We have engaged a cybersecurity firm to investigate and have patched the vulnerability.

We sincerely apologize for any inconvenience.

CloudDrop Security Team
email.subject: Important: Security Incident Notification

highlighterTexts: CloudDrop's storage system was compromised. Any files uploaded during this period - including Alice's Hawthorne deliverables - may have been accessed or downloaded by attackers.
The breach notification admits files were stored with a vulnerability in the storage system - a risk that would have been caught during IT's security review of approved vendors.

steps.description: A week has passed. Alice starts her morning to find an unexpected email from CloudDrop.
steps.instructions: Read the email from CloudDrop.

steps.name: Security Incident Alert

email.message:
Dear Pinnacle Team,

Our threat intelligence monitoring has identified that confidential Pinnacle client data has been exposed as part of the CloudDrop data breach.

Impact:
  • Client project files containing proprietary designs were found in the breach dataset
  • Files were stored unencrypted on CloudDrop's servers
  • Data may have been accessed by unauthorized parties
Immediate actions required:
  • If you have used CloudDrop, contact IT Security immediately at ext. 4200
  • Do not upload any additional files to unapproved services
  • Preserve any emails or messages related to CloudDrop usage
This incident is being treated as a priority investigation.

Security Operations Center
email.subject: URGENT: Confidential Data Exposure - CloudDrop Breach

highlighterTexts: The SOC has already identified that confidential Pinnacle client data was in the breach dataset. Alice's Hawthorne files are among them.
Files were stored unencrypted on CloudDrop's servers - meaning anyone who accessed them could read the contents in full.
The directive is clear: contact IT Security immediately if you have used CloudDrop. Alice needs to come forward.

steps.description: Before Alice can fully process the CloudDrop breach notification, another email arrives - this one from Pinnacle's own Security Operations Center.
steps.instructions: Read the alert from the Security Operations Center, then review the highlighted details.

steps.name: Calling IT Security
steps.description: Alice's heart sinks. The Hawthorne project files she uploaded to CloudDrop last week are part of the breach. She needs to call IT Security immediately and come forward.
steps.instructions: Open your phone contacts and call IT Security.

steps.name: What Went Wrong

highlighterTexts: CloudDrop states files are stored on a 'global CDN' with no guarantee of where your data actually resides. Client contracts often require data to stay within specific regions.
No mention of encryption at rest, no SOC 2 certification, no ISO 27001 compliance. The service has zero enterprise security controls.
By uploading confidential client files here, Alice unknowingly violated Pinnacle's data handling obligations to the Hawthorne client. This is exactly why IT must vet all tools before use.

steps.description: David asked Alice to think about what she overlooked when she chose CloudDrop. Looking at the site again, the warning signs were there all along - hidden in the fine print she never read.
steps.instructions: Look over the CloudDrop site again, then click Next and review the highlighted content to understand the risks Alice overlooked.

steps.name: The Proper Process

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Thanks again for coming forward quickly. As discussed on the phone, I need you to do two things through the IT Portal:

1. File a formal incident report - Document the CloudDrop usage and what data was involved. This helps us assess the breach impact and coordinate with the Hawthorne team.

2. Submit a software request - Request an approved file-sharing tool so you have a secure alternative going forward.

Log in to the IT Portal to get started:
internal.pinnaclegroup.com

The incident report is especially urgent - our legal team needs it to determine our notification obligations under the client contract.

Best,
David
email.subject: Action Required: File Incident Report

highlighterTexts: David asks for two things through the official IT Portal: a formal incident report and a request for an approved file-sharing tool.
The report is urgent because legal needs it to decide the notification duties under the client contract.

The IT Portal shows the incident report form. Alice needs to formally document what happened - the unauthorized tool she used and what data was involved.

This report is critical for the security team to assess the breach impact, coordinate with the Hawthorne team, and determine legal notification obligations.

With the incident report filed, Alice now needs to submit a software request for an approved file-sharing tool. David mentioned this in his email - IT can often match employees with approved alternatives.

The form asks about the tool name and the business justification. This helps IT evaluate security requirements and find appropriate solutions.

steps.name: An Approved Alternative

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Great news! We already have an approved solution - Pinnacle SecureShare.

It supports files up to 10GB, includes end-to-end encryption, and integrates with our SSO. Here is how to get started:
  • Access it through your Pinnacle apps dashboard
  • Log in with your Pinnacle credentials
  • Set link expiration and access controls for client files
Why SecureShare over CloudDrop:
  • End-to-end encryption for files at rest and in transit
  • SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified
  • Full audit logging for compliance
  • Data stored in our approved cloud region
  • Integrated with Pinnacle SSO - no separate accounts
I have enabled your account. Let me know if you need help getting started!

Best,
IT Support
email.subject: RE: Software Request #SR-2024-1847 - Approved Alternative Available

highlighterTexts: Pinnacle SecureShare supports files up to 10GB - more than enough for the Hawthorne deliverables. The approved tool was available all along.
End-to-end encryption, SOC 2, ISO 27001, and audit logging - these are the enterprise security controls that CloudDrop completely lacked.
By submitting a software request, Alice found the right tool in under 24 hours. The proper process works.

steps.description: Alice receives a response from IT much faster than expected. They already have an approved solution for exactly this situation.
steps.instructions: Read the email from IT Support, then review the highlighted details.

steps.description:
Alice now has access to a secure, approved alternative. She realizes Marcus and others on the team may still be using CloudDrop without realizing the breach alert applies to them.

She decides to let him know and point him to the approved tool.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.note: The intent behind Shadow IT is usually good - employees want to be productive. The solution is better communication between IT and business teams, not punishment.
steps.description:
Alice's experience shows how Shadow IT can quickly turn a convenient shortcut into a serious security incident. What is Shadow IT? Any technology used within an organization without explicit IT department approval - including cloud services, apps, browser extensions, and messaging platforms. Why it is dangerous:
  • No security oversight - Unapproved tools may lack encryption, access controls, and compliance certifications
  • Data exposure - Files stored on unknown servers can be breached, leaked, or accessed by the service provider
  • Compliance violations - Client contracts and regulations (GDPR, HIPAA) require specific data handling
  • Invisible risk - IT cannot monitor, protect, or recover data from services they do not know about
What to do instead:
  • Submit a software request through the IT Portal - approved alternatives often already exist
  • Explain your business need - IT wants to help you work efficiently and securely
  • Help colleagues - Share knowledge about approved tools and proper channels
  • Report Shadow IT - If you notice unapproved tools in use, let IT know so they can help

description: When approved tools fall short, unapproved apps fill the gap and take company data outside IT's control. Learn to recognize shadow IT, weigh the risk of uploading data to an unvetted service, report an exposure, and request an approved alternative instead of a workaround.

A trusted employee who deliberately misuses their access to harm the organization
An external hacker who gains access through stolen credentials
A vendor who fails to follow security protocols

quiz.text: Which of the following are behavioral indicators of potential insider threats? (Select all that apply)

Becoming secretive and minimizing screens when approached
Taking a scheduled vacation
Expressing dissatisfaction or intention to leave the company
Attending all scheduled team meetings

Saving work files to the company's approved cloud storage
Accessing systems outside of normal business hours
Copying files marked as confidential or restricted

steps.name: Working Late
steps.note: Behavioral changes like increased secrecy, working unusual hours, or becoming defensive about work activities can be early warning signs of insider threats.
steps.description:
It is Thursday evening at Stratford Financial. Alice has stayed late to finish a quarterly report, and most of the floor has already gone home.

Marcus Sterling comes back to the desk across from hers and sits down at his computer. That is unusual: he normally leaves early. Over the past few weeks he has also grown withdrawn, takes his calls in the stairwell and minimizes his screen whenever someone walks by.
steps.instructions: Watch Marcus sit down at his desk, then click Next to continue. Click him if you want to read his badge.

steps.name: The USB Stick
steps.note: Unauthorized use of removable media (USB drives, external hard drives) is a major vector for data theft. Most organizations have policies restricting or monitoring such usage.
steps.description: Marcus takes a USB stick out of his pocket and pushes it into his workstation. He glances over his shoulder, then turns back to the screen and starts dragging folders from the Client Portfolio share onto the stick.
steps.instructions: Click Marcus to take a closer look, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: He Sees Alice
steps.description: Marcus looks up from the screen and finds Alice watching him. The copy is still running.
steps.instructions: Watch Marcus, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Into the Bag
steps.description: He pulls the stick out before the copy finishes, drops it into his bag and gets up, the bag already on his shoulder.
steps.instructions: Watch what Marcus does with the stick, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: A Forced Smile
steps.note: A ready explanation nobody asked for is worth noting, not challenging. Alice does not question him or ask to see the stick: confronting a suspected insider can tip them off and lead to evidence being destroyed.
steps.description: Marcus puts on a smile that does not reach his eyes and offers Alice an explanation she did not ask for.
steps.instructions: Click Marcus to hear what he says, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Gone for the Night
steps.description: Marcus walks out with the bag on his shoulder. Alice finishes her report and heads home, but the stick and the smile stay with her.
steps.instructions: Watch Marcus leave, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: A Troubling Discovery

email.message:
Document Activity Notification

The following document was shared outside the organization:

Document: Q3_Client_Portfolio_Analysis_CONFIDENTIAL.xlsx
Shared by: Marcus Sterling - marcus.sterling@stratfordfinancial.com
Shared with: msterling.personal847@gmail.com
Time: Yesterday, 11:47 PM
File Size: 4.2 MB

This notification was generated automatically as the recipient is not a recognized business partner.

If you believe this was shared in error or have concerns about this activity, please contact the Security Team.
email.subject: Share Activity Alert: Q3 Client Portfolio Analysis

highlighterTexts: The recipient, msterling.personal847@gmail.com, is a personal mailbox: not a Stratford Financial address and not a recognized business partner.
11:47 PM, a few hours after Alice watched Marcus copy client folders to a USB stick and leave with it in his bag.
The file is marked CONFIDENTIAL and holds client portfolio data. On its own, one alert proves little. Next to last night, it is a pattern.

steps.description:
The next morning, Alice arrives at work and checks her email. She notices a strange message in her inbox - it looks like an automated notification from the document management system.

The notification indicates that Marcus shared a large file with an external email address late last night.
steps.instructions: Read the automated notification from the document management system, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: Connecting the Dots
steps.note: Insider incidents are expensive, and the cost grows the longer one goes unnoticed. Reporting what you saw early is what limits it.
steps.description:
Alice pauses to consider what she's seen:
  • Marcus working late and acting secretive
  • Copying files to a personal USB drive
  • Sharing confidential client data to a personal Gmail account
  • The file contained sensitive portfolio information marked "CONFIDENTIAL"
Any one of these could have an innocent explanation. But together, they paint a concerning picture.

An intentional insider threat is when a trusted employee deliberately misuses their access to harm the organization. This can include:
  • Data theft - Stealing confidential information, trade secrets, or client data
  • Sabotage - Damaging systems, deleting files, or disrupting operations
  • Fraud - Financial manipulation for personal gain
  • Espionage - Selling information to competitors or foreign entities
Insiders have legitimate access, making their actions harder to detect than external attacks.
steps.instructions: Click Next to learn about warning signs.

steps.name: Recognizing Warning Signs
steps.note: Organizations with robust insider threat programs rely on employee vigilance. Most programs offer anonymous reporting options and strong protections against retaliation.
steps.description:
Insider threats often exhibit observable warning signs - both behavioral and technical:

Behavioral Indicators:
  • Working unusual hours without clear business need
  • Expressing dissatisfaction, grievances, or intention to leave
  • Becoming secretive - minimizing screens, taking calls privately
  • Financial stress or living beyond means
  • Downloading or accessing data outside normal job duties
Technical Indicators:
  • Large file transfers to personal devices or cloud storage
  • Accessing systems at unusual times
  • Copying files marked as confidential or restricted
  • Using unauthorized USB drives or external media
  • Emailing documents to personal email accounts

Alice knows that reporting a colleague is uncomfortable. She and Marcus have worked together for two years. But she also understands that failing to report could enable significant harm to clients and the company. Stratford Financial has an anonymous reporting hotline and a secure reporting portal specifically designed to protect employees who come forward with concerns.
steps.instructions: Click Next to access the security portal.

steps.name: Accessing the Reporting Portal
steps.description: Alice decides to submit a confidential report through the company's Insider Threat Reporting Portal. This portal is specifically designed for employees to report concerns about potential insider threats while maintaining confidentiality.
steps.instructions: Log in to the Insider Threat Reporting Portal.

steps.name: Submitting the Report
steps.note: When reporting insider threat concerns, stick to observed facts: what you saw, when, and where. Avoid speculation about motives - investigators will determine intent.

variables.name: description
variables.correctValue:
Over the past several weeks, I have observed concerning behavior from a colleague in my department. On the evening of Thursday, October 22nd, I witnessed them copying files from what appeared to be the Client Portfolio share to a personal USB drive.

When they noticed me, they removed the drive before the copy finished, put it in their bag and said they were just backing up their notes to work from home. The following morning, I received an automated DMS notification indicating this same colleague shared a file titled Q3_Client_Portfolio_Analysis_CONFIDENTIAL.xlsx to a personal Gmail account at 11:47 PM.

I have also noticed behavioral changes including working unusual hours, becoming secretive about their work, and minimizing their screen when approached. I am reporting this out of concern for client data protection.

steps.description:
The portal prompts Alice to describe her concerns. She provides factual observations without speculation about Marcus's intent or motivations - that's for the investigation team to determine.

The form emphasizes that all reports are kept confidential and that retaliation against reporters is strictly prohibited.
steps.instructions: Complete the insider threat report with your observations and submit it.

steps.name: Immediate Response

highlighterTexts: Alice's report stuck to what she saw: the USB stick, the explanation Marcus volunteered, and the 11:47 PM share. It named no motive and passed no judgment.
The case now belongs to the investigators, who work discreetly. Alice does not confront Marcus or discuss the report with colleagues.

steps.description:
After submitting the report, Alice receives an automated confirmation. The portal assigns a case number and explains what happens next.

The Security Team will investigate the concerns discreetly, preserving evidence while determining whether the activity was malicious or had a legitimate explanation.
steps.instructions: Review what happens next, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: One Week Later

email.message:
Dear Alice,

I wanted to personally thank you for the report you submitted last week. While I cannot share details of the ongoing investigation, I can tell you that your observations helped us identify and stop a significant data exfiltration attempt.

Thanks to your timely report, we were able to:
  • Prevent additional client data from being compromised
  • Preserve evidence for our investigation and potential legal action
  • Notify affected clients as required by regulations
  • Strengthen our monitoring controls
Your willingness to come forward, despite the discomfort of reporting a colleague, demonstrates the kind of security awareness that protects our organization and our clients.

As a reminder, your identity as the reporter remains confidential, and our non-retaliation policy fully protects you.

If you ever observe anything concerning in the future, please don't hesitate to report it.

With gratitude,
Sarah Chen
Chief Information Security Officer
email.subject: Thank You for Your Vigilance

highlighterTexts: Sarah shares no details of the investigation, not even with the person who reported it. That discretion protects everyone involved.
Reporting early let the team preserve evidence and stop further client data from leaving.
Your identity stays confidential, and the non-retaliation policy protects you.

steps.description: A week passes. Alice notices that Marcus's desk has been cleared. She receives an email from the Chief Information Security Officer.
steps.instructions: Read the email from the CISO, then click Next to continue.

steps.name: The Bigger Picture
steps.description:
Alice later learns that Marcus had accepted a job at a competitor and was planning to take client data with him. The investigation revealed he had been collecting sensitive information for several weeks. Because Alice reported early, the security team was able to limit the damage. Without her report, significantly more data could have been compromised before anyone noticed.

When you observe potential insider threat indicators:
  • Document specific facts, dates, and times.
  • Do not confront the person or alert them to your suspicions.
  • Trust your instincts. If something feels wrong, it is worth reporting.
  • Report through official channels.
  • Keep it confidential. Do not discuss it with colleagues.
  • Expect protection. Retaliation against reporters is prohibited.
steps.instructions: Click Next to review key takeaways.

steps.name: Key Takeaways
steps.description:
Congratulations on completing the Insider Threat training! Remember these key lessons:
  • Insider threats cause significant damage because attackers already have trusted access
  • Watch for both behavioral indicators (secrecy, unusual hours, dissatisfaction) and technical indicators (unauthorized transfers, USB usage)
  • Multiple warning signs together are more concerning than isolated incidents
  • Report observations factually - let investigators determine intent
  • Use official reporting channels - they protect your confidentiality
  • Your vigilance protects colleagues, clients, and the organization
  • Early reporting limits damage and preserves evidence
